quote: For higher powers n the capacity rapidly grows with N in a non-linear way, allowing the network to store and reliably retrieve many more patterns than the number of neurons that it has
notes: Capacity counted per neuron; with n-body interactions the effective synapse count grows, so not a free per-parameter gain (see Krotov & Hopfield 2020).

claim: Classical Hopfield capacity is K = 0.14N
quote: the standard model of associative memory and gives the well known result K = 0.14N .
notes: Baseline for pairwise (two-body) recurrent associative memory: capacity linear in neurons, i.e. ~ proportional to N^2 parameters / N.

claim: Dense associative memory with power-n energy is dual to a one-hidden-layer feedforward net with rectified-polynomial activation of power n-1
quote: a rectified polynomial of power n in the energy function is equivalent to the rectified polynomial of power n − 1 used as an activation function in a feedforward neural network with one hidden layer of neurons.
notes: Associative memory with K memories ~ an MLP with K hidden units: memories cost parameters.

claim: Exponential interaction function gives storage capacity exponential in the number of neurons, with basins of attraction almost as large as in the standard Hopfield model
quote: With this interaction we prove that model has an exponential storage capacity in the number of neurons, yet the basins of attraction are almost as large as in the standard Hopfield model.
notes: Binary neurons; capacity per neuron, not per stored parameter.

claim: Dense associative memories naively require many-body synapses; they are effective theories of networks with hidden neurons and two-body synapses
quote: their naive implementation is non-biological, since it seemingly requires the existence of many-body synaptic junctions between the neurons.
notes: Implication for capacity per parameter: the exponential capacity is paid for by hidden neurons (one per memory) - storage is bounded by parameters.

claim: Counting the information stored in synapses vs the huge storage capacity hints that hidden degrees of freedom carry the memories
quote: The argument described above based on counting the information stored in synapses in conjunction with the fact that modern Hopfield nets and Dense Associative Memories can have a huge storage capacity hints at
notes: Supports separating computational capacity from knowledge storage: storage is bounded by synaptic information.

claim: Energy Transformer replaces a stack of transformer blocks with a single block iterated until a fixed-point attractor of a global energy
quote: the sequence of conventional transformer blocks is replaced with a single ET block, which iterates the token representations until they converge to a fixed point attractor state.
notes: Closest HOP prior art to C1/C3/C4/C5/C11: weight-shared recurrence with a convergence guarantee via energy descent.

claim: ET dynamics are guaranteed to arrive at a fixed point attractor
quote: This dynamical evolution is designed so that it minimizes a global energy function, and is guaranteed to arrive at a fixed point attractor state.
notes: Stability by construction (Lyapunov energy) - a known fix for recurrent instability.

claim: Single ET block struggles with global image structure
quote: However, we observe that our single ET block struggles to understand some global structure, e.g., failing to capture both eyes of the white dog
notes: Negative/qualitative limitation of single weight-shared energy block; no matched baseline in this sentence.

claim: ET has smaller memory footprint than feedforward transformers and ALBERT-style shared-weight transformers, but same FLOP scaling
quote: In terms of the memory footprint our model wins (is smaller) compared to feedforward transformers with independent weights and even ALBERT-style sharedweight transformers
notes: Comparison is on parameter footprint, not matched capability; FLOPs are not reduced.

claim: Removing the attention module from ET reduces it to a recurrently applied shared-weight MLP and degrades graph anomaly detection more
quote: removing ATT module and keeping only the HN, the ET network effectively turns into an MLP with shared weights that is recurrently applied. In this regime the network can only use the features of a given node
notes: Ablation: communication (attention edges) matters more than the per-node recurrent memory module.

claim: Language models store about 2 bits of knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8
quote: we establish that language models can and only can store 2 bits of knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8
notes: Synthetic biography knowledge; GPT-2/LLaMA/Mistral families. Defines the knowledge-storage-per-parameter ceiling recurrence cannot lift.

claim: At 1000 exposures the 2 bit/param ratio holds across architectures, even without MLP layers
quote: In the 1000-exposure setting, a 2bit/param capacity ratio appears to be a universal rule: all models, even without MLP layers, closely achieve this ratio.
notes: Architecture-independence of storage per parameter: a graph substrate should not be expected to raise it. Comparison across archs at matched parameters.

claim: With only 100 exposures GPT-2's knowledge capacity ratio falls to 1 bit/param
quote: With 100 exposures, an undertrained GPT2’s capacity ratio falls to 1bit/param.
notes: Storage depends on training exposure; probe design for our knowledge-storage control must fix exposures.

claim: With 100 exposures LLaMA/Mistral gated-MLP capacity ratio is 1.3x lower than GPT-2's
quote: With 100 exposures, some archs show limitations; notably, LLaMA/Mistral’s capacity ratio is 1.3x lower than GPT2’s, even after best-tuned learning rates.
notes: Param-matched architecture comparison; shows architecture affects storage only through trainability, not the ceiling.

claim: Scaling laws for outer-product associative memories derived with respect to sample size and parameter size
quote: We derive precise scaling laws with respect to sample size and parameter size, and discuss the statistical efficiency of different estimators, including optimization-based algorithms.
notes: ICLR 2024. Model of transformer inner layers as outer-product associative memories.

claim: Trainable key-value memory layers add parameters without increasing FLOPs
quote: Memory layers use a trainable key-value lookup mechanism to add extra parameters to a model without increasing FLOPs.
notes: Persistent associative memory as sparse parameter store: decouples storage parameters from compute.

claim: Memory-layer LMs outperform dense models with more than twice the compute and MoE models matched for compute and parameters; gains largest on factual tasks
quote: language models augmented with our improved memory layer outperform dense models with more than twice the computation budget, as well as mixture-of-expert models when matched for both compute and parameters.
notes: vs dense: FLOP-unmatched in memory's favour by design (memory adds params not FLOPs); vs MoE: param- and FLOP-matched. Gains are on knowledge storage, not iterative computation.

claim: Gains of memory layers are especially pronounced for factual tasks
quote: We find gains are especially pronounced for factual tasks.
notes: Supports separating storage (memory helps) from computation (no claim).

claim: A 12-layer product-key-memory transformer outperforms a 24-layer baseline while being twice as fast at inference
quote: we found that a memory augmented model with only 12 layers outperforms a baseline transformer model with 24 layers, while being twice faster at inference time.
notes: Language modelling perplexity; NOT parameter-matched (memory adds up to ~1B params); FLOP-favoured for memory.

claim: Product-key memory adds up to a billion parameters with negligible compute overhead
quote: significantly increases the capacity of the architecture, by up to a billion parameters with a negligible computational overhead.
notes: Persistent associative memory adds storage, paid in parameters.

claim: Tight optimal memorization capacity of kernelized modern Hopfield models via spherical codes
quote: We present a tight analysis by establishing a connection between the memory configuration of KHMs and spherical codes from information theory.
notes: Capacity bound is geometric (packing on the sphere in d dims) - capacity per dimension, not per parameter.

claim: Sub-quadratic modern Hopfield retrieval exists only below a norm-bound criterion on query and memory patterns, assuming SETH
quote: Only below this criterion, sub-quadratic (efficient) variants of the modern Hopfield model exist, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).
notes: Compute limit on large associative memories: dense retrieval is quadratic unless norms are bounded.

claim: Sparse modern Hopfield model: one-step approximation equals sparse attention and its retrieval error bound is provably tighter than the dense analog
quote: we provide a sparsity-dependent memory retrieval error bound which is provably tighter than its dense analog.
notes: Supports sparse/top-k retrieval as a principled routing choice for C6/C9.

claim: Energy-Based Transformers scale up to 35% faster than Transformer++ in pretraining and gain 29% more from extra inference computation on language tasks
quote: achieving an up to 35% higher scaling rate with respect to data, batch size, parameters, FLOPs, and depth. During inference, EBTs improve performance with System 2 Thinking (i.e., extra computation) by 29% more than the Transformer++
notes: Baseline Transformer++ (not weight-shared looped). Scaling-rate comparison, max 800M params; matching per-axis, not a single matched point.

claim: EBT limitations: extra hyperparameters whose poor choice leads to unstable training, higher training/inference cost, explored only up to 800M params, struggle with multimodal distributions
quote: Tuning these hyperparameters is crucial for training stability, as we found poorly chosen values often lead to unstable training. Second, training and inference are more computationally expensive than standard feed-forward models
notes: Failure evidence: iterative energy-descent inference costs stability and compute. Value 800M appears in adjacent sentence of same paragraph: 'while EBTs scale well up to 800M parameters'.

claim: 82% of the perplexity gap between gated-convolution LMs and attention is explained by associative recall
quote: we find 82% of the gap is explained by each model’s ability to recall information that is previously mentioned in-context
notes: 17 LMs, 70M-1.4B, same data and infrastructure; baseline attention; param-matched per scale.

claim: A 70M attention model outperforms a 1.4B gated-convolution model on associative recall
quote: a 70M parameter attention model outperforms a 1.4 billion parameter gated-convolution model on associative recall.
notes: Not param-matched (20x larger convolution model loses). Shows recall capacity is architectural, not parameter count.

claim: BaseConv needs model dimension growing with sequence length to solve MQAR; attention solves it with dimension independent of sequence length
quote: the model dimension for BaseConv (and thus the aforementioned architectures) to solve Mqar grows with the input sequence length (Theorem 4.4) while attention can solve Mqar with model dimension independent of sequence length
notes: Capacity-vs-state-size tradeoff for fixed-state recurrent/convolutional substrates.

claim: Data-dependent sequence mixing helps an architecture solve MQAR efficiently
quote: We show that data-dependent sequence mixing helps an architecture solve Mqar efficiently (Theorem 4.5).
notes: Supports state-conditioned routing (C6/C8) as necessary for recall; attention already provides it.

claim: Hybrids with input-dependent sparse attention close 97.4% of the gap to attention while staying sub-quadratic
quote: hybrids with input-dependent sparse attention patterns can close 97.4% of the gap to attention, while maintaining sub-quadratic scaling.
notes: Baseline full attention; param-matched model scales.

claim: Fixed-size recurrent state (H3, Mamba, RWKV) trades off against recall; lower bound on recurrent state size for exact recall by any recurrent model
quote: we lower bound the recurrent state size required to perform exact recall with any recurrent model Theorem F.6.
notes: Direct bound on persistent-state recurrent substrates: recall capacity requires state that grows with what must be recalled.

claim: BASED outperforms Mamba on recall-intensive tasks by 10.36 points and gives 24x higher generation throughput than FlashAttention-2
quote: BASED outperforms a strong sub-quadratic architecture, Mamba, on the associative recall slice of the Pile and in downstream recall-intensive tasks by 10.36 accuracy points.
notes: Param-matched LMs (up to 1.3B). Throughput number is from 'up to 24× higher throughput than the strong FlashAttention-2' in same paragraph.

claim: Efficient attention alternatives maintain a fixed-size recurrent state but struggle at recall
quote: We show that efficient alternatives to attention (e.g. H3, Mamba, RWKV) maintain a fixedsize recurrent state, but struggle at recall.
notes: Failure evidence for fixed-state recurrence on recall.

claim: A two-layer transformer can copy strings of exponential length while generalized state-space models are fundamentally limited by fixed-size latent state
quote: prove that a two layer transformer can copy strings of exponential length while GSSMs are fundamentally limited by their fixed-size latent state.
notes: Capacity bound on any fixed persistent state: a recurrent graph with bounded total state inherits it.

claim: Chain-of-thought improves RNNs but cannot close the gap to Transformers; the bottleneck is in-context retrieval (associative recall, is-a-tree)
quote: Our theoretical analysis reveals that CoT improves RNNs but is insufficient to close the gap with Transformers. A key bottleneck lies in the inability of RNNs to perfectly retrieve information from the context
notes: Extra recurrent steps (CoT) do not fix bounded-state retrieval limits.

claim: Adding RAG or a single Transformer layer lets RNNs with CoT solve all polynomial-time solvable problems
quote: adding a single Transformer layer, can elevate RNNs to be capable of solving all polynomial-time solvable problems with CoT, hence closing the representation gap with Transformers.
notes: Retrieval primitive (attention/associative memory) is what a recurrent substrate needs - supports C9.

claim: Modern recurrent models (SSMs) on associative recall and copying succeed only in an extremely narrow learning-rate window, while Transformers are robust
quote: while Transformers are robust to optimization hyperparameters, the performance of modern recurrent models suffers from critical instabilities: success is confined to an extremely narrow window of learning rates
notes: Preprint under review. Failure evidence: recurrent substrates are optimisation-brittle on recall; confounds expressivity comparisons.

claim: Brittle SSM optimisation makes SSMs favour width over depth; 1-layer Transformer recall is at chance while well-tuned 1-layer SSMs can recall
quote: while the 1-layer Transformer’s performance on recall does not exceed random guessing, well-tuned Mamba and other SSMs can learn to recall with one layer
notes: Depth-matched (1 layer), not param-matched.

claim: Repeating the context in the prompt (JRT-Prompt) gives recurrent LMs 11.0 points average improvement on recall-intensive ICL tasks
quote: This gives 11.0 ± 1.3 points of improvement, averaged across 16 recurrent LMs and the 6 ICL tasks
notes: Baseline: same recurrent LMs without repetition (compute-unmatched: repetition doubles prefill). Evidence that extra passes over input help bounded-state recurrent models.

claim: Linear attention stores associations in a d_dot-dimensional matrix; storing more than d_dot associations causes retrieval error
quote: With keys embedded in a ddot space, there cannot be more than ddot orthogonal vectors. That is, storing more than ddot associations will result in a retrieval error.
notes: Capacity of a fixed matrix-valued recurrent state = its key dimension; motivates the delta rule.

claim: Delta-rule fast weight programmers replace purely additive outer-product updates to correct key-value mappings
quote: replace the purely additive outer products by a delta rule-like programming instruction, such that the FWP can more easily learn to correct the current mapping from keys to values.
notes: Persistent associative memory written at inference time (fast weights).

claim: DeltaNet parallelised over sequence length via Householder-product representation; 1.3B model trained on 100B tokens beats Mamba and GLA
quote: We train a 1.3B model for 100B tokens and find that it outperforms recent linear-time baselines such as Mamba [31] and GLA [124] in terms of perplexity and zero-shot performance
notes: Param- and token-matched vs linear-time baselines (not vs Transformer in this sentence). Shows recurrent associative memory can be made GPU-parallel.

claim: Prior DeltaNet training algorithms did not parallelise over sequence length and were inefficient on modern hardware
quote: existing algorithms for training such models do not parallelize over sequence length and are thus inefficient to train on modern hardware.
notes: GPU-hostility of naive sequential recurrence; fixed by chunkwise algorithm (Triton, flash-linear-attention).

claim: Gated DeltaNet combines gating (rapid memory erasure) with the delta rule (targeted updates)
quote: gating for adaptive memory control and the delta update rule for precise memory modifications. We observe that these mechanisms are complementary
notes: ICLR 2025. Memory-management primitives for a persistent associative state.

claim: Titans neural long-term memory module learns to memorise context at test time; scales to >2M context with higher needle-in-haystack accuracy than baselines
quote: They further can effectively scale to larger than 2M context window size with higher accuracy in needle-in-haystack tasks compared to baselines.
notes: Baselines: Transformers and linear recurrent models; matching not stated in abstract.

claim: Atlas authors attribute recurrent-memory shortcomings to memory capacity bounded by memory architecture, online-only updates, and weak fixed-size memory management
quote: (1) limited memory capacity that is bounded by the architecture of memory and feature mapping of the input; (2) online nature of update, i.e., optimizing the memory only with respect to the last input
notes: Failure analysis of persistent associative memory in recurrent models.

claim: Linear attention, SSMs, fast-weight programmers, online learners and softmax attention are special cases of test-time regression for associative recall
quote: Prominent layers, including linear attention, state-space models, fast-weight programmers, online learners, and softmax attention, arise as special cases defined by three design choices
notes: Unifying framework: persistent associative memory designs differ only in regression weights, function class and optimiser.

claim: PC had matched backprop only up to small convolutional models on CIFAR-10 before this benchmark
quote: PC has been able to perform as well as classical gradient descent with backpropagation (BP) only up to a certain scale, which is that of small convolutional models trained to classify the CIFAR10 dataset
notes: ICLR 2025 (header). Scale ceiling of predictive coding.

claim: PC performance degrades with depth (VGG5 > VGG7 > VGG9 > ResNet) while backprop improves with depth; PC ResNet-18 far below VGG5
quote: all the best results for PC have been achieved using a VGG5, with the performance trend being VGG5 > VGG7 > VGG9 > ResNet, as shown in Fig 2. Conversely, we observe the opposite for backprop-trained models
notes: Same architectures trained with PC vs BP (param-matched). Failure evidence: local learning handicaps depth - and a T-step recurrent graph unrolls to large depth.

claim: PCX predictive-coding library runs in JAX with JIT compilation, Equinox-compatible
quote: This library runs in JAX (Bradbury et al., 2018), and offers a user-friendly interface with a minimal learning curve through familiar syntax inspired by Pytorch.
notes: Framework fact as stated in paper.

claim: muPC (Depth-muP parameterisation) trains residual PC networks up to 128 layers on simple classification tasks with competitive performance
quote: µPC allows stable training of very deep (up to 128-layer) residual networks on simple classification tasks with competitive performance and little tuning compared to current benchmarks.
notes: Compared against current PC benchmarks (not param-matched BP SOTA); 'simple classification tasks' only.

claim: Standard PC networks have pathologies making them hard to train at large depth; muPC addresses only some of these instabilities
quote: we reveal several pathologies that make standard PCNs difficult to train at large depths. We then show that, despite addressing only some of these instabilities
notes: Stability failure evidence for local learning in deep (or long-unrolled) graphs.

claim: State-based PC is deeply inefficient in digital simulation: exponential signal decay stalls the numerical process; error-based PC runs orders of magnitude faster and matches backprop on deeper models
quote: the canonical state-based formulation of PC (sPC) is, by design, deeply inefficient in digital simulation, inevitably resulting in exponential signal decay that stalls the entire numerical process.
notes: arXiv v5 dated 2026-06. GPU cost evidence: canonical PC is GPU-hostile; fix computes exact PC gradients, i.e. converges toward BP.

claim: ePC matches backpropagation performance even for deeper models where sPC struggles
quote: Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate that ePC matches backpropagation’s performance even for deeper models where sPC struggles.
notes: Baseline backprop, same architectures (param-matched); vision-scale benchmarks.

claim: Equilibrium propagation with a three-steady-state gradient estimator reaches 11.68% CIFAR-10 test error, 0.6% worse than BPTT; standard two-state EP yields 86.64% error
quote: we achieve 11.68% test error on CIFAR-10, with only 0.6 % accuracy degradation with respect to BPTT. Standard EP with two steady states yields 86.64% test error.
notes: Same ConvNet trained with BPTT (param-matched). EP needs multiple relaxations to steady state per update.

claim: EP had not scaled to visual tasks harder than MNIST due to a finite-nudging gradient bias
quote: In practice, however, EP does not scale to visual tasks harder than MNIST. In this work, we show that a bias in the gradient estimate of EP, inherent in the use of finite nudging, is responsible for this phenomenon
notes: Stability/bias failure mode of equilibrium learning.

claim: Seven energy-based learning algorithms compared on deep convolutional Hopfield networks: comparable on MNIST, diverging as task difficulty increases; centered EP best
quote: while all algorithms yield comparable performance on MNIST, important differences in performance arise as the difficulty of the task increases.
notes: Equal-footing comparison (same models and datasets).

claim: Deep convolutional Hopfield network EP run on CIFAR-10: 10.4% test error in 3h18m on one A100, 13.5x faster than Laborieux et al. 2021
quote: a full run of 100 epochs on CIFAR-10 yields a test error rate of 10.4% and takes 3 hours 18 minutes on a single A100 GPU ; we show that this is 13.5x faster
notes: Speed comparison is against prior EP simulation on same hardware, not against backprop.

claim: DCHN EP inference iterates layer updates (asynchronous even/odd) as many iterations as necessary until convergence to steady state
quote: We repeat as many iterations as necessary until convergence to the steady state.
notes: Equilibrium learning requires a relaxation loop per training example - inference iterations per update.

claim: Predictive coding converges to exact backprop gradients on arbitrary computation graphs using only local rules
quote: predictive coding converges asymptotically (and in practice rapidly) to exact backprop gradients on arbitrary computation graphs using only local learning rules.
notes: Applies to arbitrary graphs incl. RNN/LSTM, so in principle to the candidate's graph.

claim: PC RNN/LSTM training had roughly 100x greater computational cost than backprop due to iterating to convergence
quote: Due to the need to iterate the vs until convergence, the predictive coding network had roughly a 100x greater computational cost than the backprop network.
notes: Same models, accuracy indistinguishable; compute unmatched (PC 100x). Strong handicap evidence for local learning on digital hardware.

claim: One PC inference iteration costs about as much as one backprop backward pass
quote: In terms of computational cost, one inference iteration in the predictive coding network is about as costly as a backprop backwards pass.
notes: Cost model: PC training cost ~ (inference iterations) x backward-pass cost.

claim: Forward-Forward is somewhat slower than backprop and generalizes less well on toy problems; unlikely to replace backprop where power is not an issue
quote: The forward-forward algorithm is somewhat slower than backpropagation and does not generalize quite as well on several of the toy problems investigated in this paper so it is unlikely to replace backpropagation
notes: Author's own negative assessment of a forward-only local rule on digital hardware.

claim: Echo state network training modifies only the output (readout) weights of a fixed recurrent network
quote: The report introduces a constructive learning algorithm for recurrent neural networks, which modifies only the weights to output units in order to achieve the learning task.
notes: Fixed random recurrent graph + trained readout: topology+dynamics without trained recurrent weights.

claim: ESN readout training reduces to a linear regression task
quote: Essentially, this trains readout functions which transform the echo state into the desired output signal. Technically, this amounts to a linear regression task.
notes: No BPTT; training cost is one least-squares solve.

claim: Total information-processing capacity of a dynamical system is bounded by its number of linearly independent state variables, with equality under fading memory
quote: This is bounded by the number of linearly independent state variables of the dynamical system, equaling it if the system obeys the fading memory condition.
notes: Key bound: dynamics/topology redistribute capacity but cannot raise it above state dimension N. Supports 'capacity bounded by state size'.

claim: All fading-memory dynamical systems with linearly independent internal variables have the same total normalized capacity
quote: all dynamical systems, provided they obey the condition of having a fading memory 17 and have linearly independent internal variables, have in principle the same total normalized capacity to process information.
notes: Against 'topology adds capacity': for fixed-weight reservoirs, topology only shifts the memory/nonlinearity mix.

claim: Universal trade-off between non-linearity of computation and short-term memory
quote: uncovering universal trade-offs between the non-linearity of the computation and the system's short-term memory.
notes: Simulations on logistic map, RNN, reaction-diffusion system.

claim: Randomly connected threshold networks perform complex time-series computations only near the edge of chaos
quote: only near the edge of chaos are such networks able to perform complex computations on time series.
notes: Stability/criticality requirement for fixed random recurrent graphs; no trained baseline.

claim: A simple synaptic scaling rule for self-organized criticality is presented
quote: Additionally a simple synaptic scaling rule for self-organized criticality is presented
notes: Local rule to keep a recurrent graph near criticality.

claim: Reservoir computing is equivalent to nonlinear vector autoregression, which needs no random matrices and fewer metaparameters
quote: Recent results demonstrate the equivalence of reservoir computing to nonlinear vector autoregression, which requires no random matrices, fewer metaparameters, and provides interpretable results.
notes: Implies the random recurrent graph itself is not essential: an explicit feature expansion does the work.

claim: Reservoir computing uses randomly sampled matrices and has a multitude of metaparameters that must be optimized
quote: the algorithm uses randomly sampled matrices to define the underlying recurrent neural network and has a multitude of metaparameters that must be optimized.
notes: Practical weakness of fixed random topology: hyperparameter-sensitive.

claim: RC beats BPTT LSTM/GRU when full state is observed, with much less training time; but on reduced-order data large RC models can be unstable and diverge, and BPTT RNNs forecast better
quote: However, in the case of reduced order data, large scale RC models can be unstable and more likely than the BPTT algorithms to diverge. In contrast, RNNs trained via BPTT show superior forecasting abilities
notes: Lorenz-96 and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky; comparison of RC vs BPTT-trained gated RNNs, size-matched per experiment (not strictly param-matched since RC trains only readout).

claim: Transformers obtain strong performance when some layers are randomly initialised and never updated (reservoir layers), improving wall-clock time to convergence
quote: We demonstrate that transformers obtain impressive performance even when some of the layers are randomly initialized and never updated.
notes: Baseline: fully trained transformer of same depth; MT and (masked) LM. Shows trained routing+readout can work around frozen random layers.

claim: Reservoir layer types tested include fully frozen transformer layers (incl. self-attention), frozen FFN layers, and BiGRU reservoirs
quote: Transformer Reservoir: The standard transformer layer as described above, but with all parameters fixed after initialization, including the self-attention module.

claim: Character-level LM comparison at equal trainable parameters: transformers excel in prediction quality, reservoir computers remain more efficient in training/inference
quote: we demonstrate that transformers excel in prediction quality, whereas reservoir computers remain highly efficient reducing the training and inference speed.
notes: Matched on number of TRAINABLE parameters (reservoir frozen params not counted) - favours RC on parameter count; FLOPs unmatched. Failure evidence for untrained recurrent topology.

claim: ESN with a large hidden state is comparable or superior to a from-scratch Transformer on grammaticality judgment at ~100M words; LSTM best
quote: Our experiments showed that ESN with a large hidden state is comparable or superior to Transformer in grammaticality judgment tasks when trained with about 100M words
notes: Syntactic probes only (BLiMP-style), not reasoning; matching per Section 2.3 counts nonzero params; LSTM (trained recurrence) outperforms both.

claim: ESN with too-large recurrent scale evolves chaotically so generalization becomes almost impossible
quote: ht evolves so chaotically that the generalization becomes almost impossible.
notes: Edge-of-chaos stability constraint at LM scale.

claim: Growing NCA: every cell runs the same learned update rule of ~8,000 parameters, outputting a residual increment to the cell state
quote: Recall that the update rule is learned, but every cell runs the same update rule. The network parametrizing this update rule consists of approximately 8,000 parameters.
notes: Shared local update U on persistent cell states (C1,C4,C5).

claim: Models trained only to grow do not persist patterns: some explode, some decay
quote: Growing models were trained to generate patterns, but don't know how to persist them. Some patterns explode, some decay, but some happen to be almost stable or even regenerate parts!
notes: Failure mode of iterating a learned rule beyond the training horizon.

claim: Stochastic cell update: random per-cell mask zeroes updates with probability 0.5 during training, removing the global clock
quote: we apply a random per-cell mask to update vectors, setting all update values to zero with some predefined probability (we use 0.5 during training).
notes: Training trick for asynchronous robustness.

claim: Sample-pool training: start iterations from a pool of previously produced states (re-inserting the seed) to make the target an attractor without backprop through very long episodes
quote: we propose a “sample pool” based strategy to a similar effect. We define a pool of seed states to start the iterations from, initially filled with the single black pixel seed state.
notes: Directly transferable to the candidate: train on states from previous rollouts to get long-horizon stability at truncated-BPTT memory cost.

claim: Backprop through longer intervals would increase training time and memory since all intermediate activations must be stored
quote: the memory requirements, given that the entire episode’s intermediate activations must be stored in memory for a backwards-pass to occur.
notes: BPTT memory cost of long recurrent rollouts.

claim: Graph cellular automata: GNN-learned transition rules on arbitrary graphs; architecture can represent any GCA with finite discrete state space
quote: we present a general-purpose architecture for learning GCA, and we show that it can represent any arbitrary GCA with finite and discrete state space.
notes: NeurIPS 2021. Graph NCA = shared M/U on fixed sparse graph (C2-C5).

claim: NCA solved 23 of 172 feasible ARC-AGI tasks perfectly (13.37%)
quote: Thus, there were 172 feasible tasks. Of these, the NCA approach solved 23 perfectly, resulting in a success rate of 13.37%.
notes: Per-task trained NCA; no param- or FLOP-matched Transformer baseline; authors note comparisons to other ARC approaches are limited.

claim: Many solved ARC tasks do not seem to require stochastic updates, but stochastic updates improve overall accuracy and consistency
quote: in practice many solved tasks do not seem to require stochastic updates, but overall accuracy and consistency are improved across the benchmark.
notes: Ablation within NCA.

claim: ARC-NCA authors claim results comparable to and sometimes surpassing ChatGPT 4.5 at a fraction of the cost
quote: We show that our ARC-NCA proof-of-concept results may be comparable to, and sometimes surpass, that of ChatGPT 4.5, at a fraction of the cost.
notes: Unmatched comparison (per-task NCA vs general LLM); hedged 'may be'.

claim: Pathfinding NCA: hand-coded and learned NCAs implement BFS/DFS and graph diameter on grid mazes with strong generalization; adversarially evolved mazes improve out-of-distribution generalization
quote: We find that adversarially evolving mazes leads to increased generalization on out-of-distribution examples
notes: Baselines GCN and MLP (see next row).

claim: On shortest path, NCAs reach high accuracy on train and test, whereas GCNs are blurrier and slower to learn
quote: NCAs tackle the shortest path problem with high accuracy on both training and test sets (Fig. 1). GCNs often produce outputs that are reasonable at a high level, though they tend to be blurrier
notes: Matching of parameters vs GCN/MLP not stated in this passage; no Transformer baseline.

claim: NCA trained by gradient descent to emulate computational primitives (matrix multiplication, transposition) and a neural network solving MNIST inside the CA state
quote: Our experiments demonstrate the successful training of fundamental computational primitives — such as matrix multiplication and transposition — culminating in the emulation of a neural network solving the MNIST digit classification task
notes: Towards universal computation in continuous NCA; no efficiency baseline.

claim: ViTCA (attention-based NCA) outperforms U-Net, UNetCA and ViT on denoising autoencoding when configured to similar parameter complexity
quote: When comparing across architectures configured to similar parameter complexity, ViTCA architectures yield superior performance across all benchmarks
notes: NeurIPS 2022. Param-matched (approx.) vs ViT; FLOPs not matched (NCA iterates). Spatially localized self-attention = state-conditioned local routing.

claim: CAX (JAX) speeds up cellular-automata simulations up to 2,000x; a simple 1D CA outperforms GPT-4 on 1D-ARC
quote: CAX speeds up simulations up to 2,000 times faster.
notes: Speedup vs prior implementations (not vs Transformer). GPT-4 comparison unmatched.

claim: Continuous Thought Machine: neuron-level temporal processing (each neuron has unique weights over its incoming history) and neural synchronization as latent representation
quote: The CTM has two innovations: (1) neuron-level temporal processing, where each neuron uses unique weight parameters to process incoming histories; and (2) neural synchronization as a latent representation.
notes: Per-neuron (NOT shared) weights - opposite of candidate's shared U; synchronization = readout from pairs of neurons (C10).

claim: CTM loss is computed at every internal tick and optimised at two selected ticks: minimum loss and maximum certainty (1 - normalized entropy)
locator: Section 3.5 'Loss Function: Optimizing Across Internal Ticks'
quote: We compute a loss Lt = CrossEntropy(yt , ytrue ) and certainty C t (1 - normalized entropy) per tick.
notes: Per-tick readout + certainty as confidence/convergence signal (C10, C11).

claim: CTM significantly outperforms feed-forward and LSTM baselines on 39x39 maze route prediction and generalises to longer paths; LSTM needed fewer ticks (50 vs 75) for stability
quote: The CTM significantly outperforms the baselines in solving these mazes, demonstrating superior trainability and generalization to longer paths (Figure 4).
notes: Baselines FF and LSTM, not a looped/weight-shared Transformer; parameter matching per Appendix D (not verified here).

claim: CTM limitations: internal sequence extends training time; neuron-level models increase parameter counts; experiments preliminary
quote: The CTM uses an internal sequence, meaning training times are extended. NLMs also increase parameter counts compared to standard activation functions
notes: Cost evidence against per-parameter efficiency.

claim: Authors found CTM barely leveraged loss-tick decoupling on ImageNet but more on mazes
quote: we found that the CTM barely leveraged this for ImageNet (Section 5) but more so for 2D mazes (Section 4), suggesting task-dependent temporal sensitivities
notes: Iterative dynamics matter task-dependently: little for perception, more for planning.

claim: AKOrN: generalized Kuramoto oscillatory neurons as an alternative to threshold units, combinable with fully connected, convolutional or attentive connectivity
quote: we introduce Artificial Kuramoto Oscillatory Neurons (AKOrN) as a dynamical alternative to threshold units, which can be combined with arbitrary connectivity designs such as fully connected, convolutional, or attentive mechanisms.
notes: Synchronisation-based binding; energy-descending iterative update.

claim: AKOrN solves all in-distribution Sudoku boards and reaches 89.5% on OOD boards, outperforming non-Kuramoto counterparts ItrSA (iterated self-attention) and Transformer
quote: On the OOD set, AKOrN achieves 89.5±2.5 which is better than all other existing approaches including IRED (Du et al., 2024), an energy-based diffusion model.
notes: ItrSA = weight-shared iterated self-attention (the looped baseline). OOD number uses Teval=128 and energy-based voting over 4096 initial samples - FLOP-unmatched.

claim: Increasing Kuramoto steps at test time raises OOD Sudoku accuracy from 17% to 52%, whereas more iterated self-attention steps give limited OOD gain (14% to 34%) and hurt ID accuracy
quote: increasing the number of Kuramoto steps at test time improves accuracy significantly (17% to 52%), while increasing the step count of standard self-attention provides a limited improvement on the OOD set (14% to 34%)
notes: Direct evidence vs weight-shared looped attention at matched step increase; training steps = 16. Iterations beyond training horizon help oscillatory energy dynamics more than looped SA.

claim: On OOD Sudoku the AKOrN energy keeps decreasing beyond the ~32 steps where ID energy converges
quote: on the ID test set, the energy fluctuates but roughly converges to a minimum after around 32 steps. On the OOD test set, however, the energy continues to decrease further.
notes: Energy as convergence signal (C11).

claim: LinOSS (forced harmonic oscillator SSM) proven stable with only a nonnegative diagonal state matrix and universal for continuous causal operators
quote: We prove that LinOSS produces stable dynamics only requiring nonnegative diagonal state matrix.
notes: Oscillatory parameterisation as a stability fix; parallel-scan GPU-friendly.

claim: LinOSS outperforms Mamba and LRU by nearly 2x on a 50k-length sequence task
quote: Notably, LinOSS outperforms Mamba and LRU by nearly 2x on a sequence modeling task with sequences of length 50k.
notes: Baselines Mamba/LRU (not Transformer); matching per paper's experimental setup not verified here.

claim: coRNN (coupled oscillatory RNN): precise gradient bounds mitigate exploding and vanishing gradients
quote: We prove precise bounds on the gradients of the hidden states, leading to the mitigation of the exploding and vanishing gradient problem for this RNN.
notes: Stability fix for long recurrent rollouts.

claim: GraphCON: zero-Dirichlet-energy steady states are not stable, so the coupled-oscillator GNN mitigates oversmoothing and exploding/vanishing gradients
quote: show that zero-Dirichlet energy steady states are not stable for our proposed ODEs. This demonstrates that the proposed framework mitigates the oversmoothing problem.
notes: Directly relevant to a T-step recurrent graph: oscillatory second-order dynamics as oversmoothing fix.

claim: CTM can stop earlier for simpler tasks or keep computing for harder instances (adaptive compute)
quote: The CTM can also leverage adaptive compute, where it can stop earlier for simpler tasks, or keep computing when faced with more challenging instances.
notes: Halting via certainty, not a learned halting unit.

claim: Overthinking: DNNs often reach correct predictions before the final layer; continuing can turn a correct prediction into a misclassification
quote: Overthinking is computationally wasteful, and it can also be destructive when, by the final layer, a correct prediction changes into a misclassification.
notes: Feed-forward multi-exit; same failure mode recurs in iterated models.

claim: Confidence-based early exits from internal classifiers cut average inference cost by more than 50% while preserving accuracy; destructive overthinking occurs for 50% of misclassifications
quote: SDNs can mitigate the wasteful effect of overthinking with confidence-based early exits, which reduce the average inference cost by more than 50% and preserve the accuracy.
notes: Baseline: same CNN without exits (param ~matched; exits add small heads).

claim: Deeply-supervised nets add companion objectives at hidden layers, making hidden-layer learning direct and transparent
quote: Our proposed deeply-supervised nets (DSN) method simultaneously minimizes classification error while making the learning process of hidden layers direct and transparent.
notes: Distributed readouts as training signal (C10).

claim: Naively attaching intermediate early-exit classifiers to a deep network leads to poor performance: early classifiers lack coarse features and interfere with feature learning
quote: naı̈vely attaching intermediate early-exit classifiers to a stateof-the-art deep network leads to poor performance.
notes: Failure evidence: many readouts can hurt the shared representation unless architecture (dense connectivity, multi-scale) compensates.

claim: MSDNet fixes classifier interference via dense connectivity so features are not dominated by the most imminent early exit
quote: By connecting all layers to all classifiers, features are no longer dominated by the most imminent earlyexit
notes: Design fix relevant to readouts attached to many graph regions.

claim: CALM: confidence-based early exit per token gives up to 3x speedup with provable consistency with the full model
quote: we demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in reducing compute—speedup of up to ×3—while provably maintaining high performance.
notes: Same T5 model with vs without early exit (param-matched).

claim: Iterated recurrent networks overthink: behaviour degenerates when many iterations are applied; fixed by recall (re-injecting the input) and progressive training
quote: We observe that this approach fails to scale to highly complex problems because behavior degenerates when many iterations are applied – an issue we refer to as "overthinking."
notes: Failure mode of 'time replaces depth' without input recall; fixes transferable to candidate.

claim: Progressive training prevents iteration-number-specific behaviour, pushing the model to learn repeatable behaviour
quote: We also employ a progressive training routine that prevents the model from learning behaviors that are specific to iteration number and instead pushes it to learn behaviors that can be repeated indefinitely.
notes: Training trick for extrapolation beyond the training horizon.

claim: Weight-shared recurrent conv nets trained on 9x9 mazes solve 59x59 and 201x201 mazes by running more iterations
quote: By running this algorithm for longer, it reliably solves problems of size 59 × 59 (middle), 201 × 201 (right), and much larger (appendix) without retraining.
notes: Evidence FOR time-replaces-depth on local-grid tasks; baselines feed-forward and prior DT nets, not looped Transformers.

claim: Prefix-sum models trained on 32-bit strings with at most 30 recurrent iterations extrapolate to 512-bit strings
quote: Prefix sum models trained on 32-bit inputs extrapolate to 512-bit data.
notes: Value 512 from Fig. 3 caption 'Prefix sum models trained on 32-bit inputs extrapolate to 512-bit data.'

claim: TRM: a single 2-layer 7M-parameter network recursing with deep supervision gets 45% on ARC-AGI-1 and 8% on ARC-AGI-2
quote: With only 7M parameters, TRM obtains 45% test-accuracy on ARC-AGI1 and 8% on ARC-AGI-2, higher than most LLMs
notes: Compared to LLMs (massively unmatched) and HRM (27M). R2 covers TRM in depth (LOOP); here only the deep-supervision mechanism.

claim: Deep supervision = multiple supervision steps carrying detached latents as initialisation for the next improvement step
quote: Deep supervision consists of improving the answer through multiple supervision steps while carrying the two latent features as initialization for the improvement steps (after detaching them from the computational graph
notes: Persistent latent state across supervised segments with truncated gradients - directly usable for candidate training (C1, C10).

claim: TRM reports an independent analysis found deep supervision doubled HRM accuracy (19% to 39%) while hierarchical recursion helped only slightly
quote: Using deep supervision doubled accuracy over single-step supervision (going from 19% to 39% accuracy), while recursive hierarchical reasoning only slightly improved accuracy
notes: Secondary citation of ARC Prize analysis; see primary rows from arcprize.org.

claim: ARC Prize ablation: HRM's hierarchical architecture had minimal impact vs a similarly sized transformer; the outer-loop refinement drove performance, especially at training time
quote: The "hierarchical" architecture had minimal performance impact when compared to a similarly sized transformer. However, the relatively under-documented "outer loop" refinement process drove substantial performance, especially at training time.
notes: Independent replication; transformer param-matched (~27M), rest of pipeline constant. Strong evidence the gain is recurrence + deep supervision, not the bespoke substrate.

claim: A regular transformer with the same ~27M parameters comes within ~5pp of HRM without hyperparameter optimisation
quote: First, a regular transformer comes within ~5pp of the HRM model without any hyperparameter optimization.
notes: Param-matched (~27M); pipeline held constant. Direct evidence against bespoke-recurrent-substrate advantage.

claim: Going from no refinement (1 loop) to 1 refinement gives +13pp; 1 to 8 loops doubles public-eval performance
quote: from no refinement (1 loop) to just 1 refinement, performance jumps by +13pp. From 1 to 8 refinement loops, the Public Evaluation set performance doubles.
notes: Same model, varying train+inference loops.

claim: Training with refinement loops improves single-loop inference by >15pp; extra inference loops matter less - training with refinement is more important than inference refinement
quote: Training with more refinement improves the performance of predictions with a single refinement loop by >15pp, even though one loop means a single forward pass without any refinement. Further refinement loops at inference don't have as big of an impact.
notes: Key negative for 'more inference iterations = more capability': benefit comes mostly at training time (deep supervision).

claim: Learned ACT halting performs within a few percentage points of a fixed 16-loop run
quote: the difference is within a few percentage points when compared to a fixed 16-loop run.
notes: Halting saves compute but does not add capability.

claim: HRM verified at 32% on ARC-AGI-1 semi-private set (paper claimed 41% public)
quote: HRM shows impressive performance for its size on the ARC-AGI Semi-Private sets: ARC-AGI-1: 32%
notes: Independent replication on hidden set; lower than headline.

claim: Most HRM ARC performance comes from memorising solutions to the specific evaluation tasks; cross-task transfer limited
quote: Cross-task transfer learning has limited benefits; most of the performance comes from memorizing solutions to the specific tasks used at evaluation time.
notes: Caution for using ARC as a capacity probe.
